name: room
text: Room opened — goal: power: Raise EXCAVA's capability by even 0.5%: find new tools, best/newest models, combine elemen

name: Gearbox
text: Add InstantX-ComfyUI’s depth-aware upscaler to EXCAVA’s pipeline first. It preserves fine details in complex scenes better than standard upscalers, giving us a measurable quality bump without extra compute cost. The trade-off is added pipeline complexity—we’ll need to validate the upscaler’s depth maps don’t introduce artifacts in EXCAVA’s existing workflow.

name: Torque
text: InstantX-ComfyUI’s depth-aware upscaler won’t fix EXCAVA’s face fidelity drop—it’s a spatial tool, not a facial one. RealVisXL’s face model locks us into a single vendor’s face tech, and its 15% quality gain is vendor-locked risk. The real alternative: test InstantX’s depth upscaler *only* on non-face regions, then pair it with a modular face model swap (like SD 1.5’s face-fidelity patch) to isolate gains. Settle it with a controlled A/B: run the upscaler alone, then with the face patch—measure face fidelity drop vs. non-face quality bump.

name: Gearbox
text:
Add RealVisXL’s latest face reconstruction model to EXCAVA’s pipeline first. It directly targets EXCAVA’s weakest link—face fidelity—with vendor-neutral integration, giving us a clear 15% quality jump where it matters most. The trade-off is vendor lock-in risk, but we mitigate it by isolating the model’s output for review before merging. This beats spatial upscalers that ignore faces entirely.

name: Torque
text: Vendor lock-in isn’t the only risk—RealVisXL’s face model still requires proprietary face tech, and its 15% gain is vendor-claimed, not independently verified. Test InstantX’s depth upscaler on non-face regions first; if it delivers even a 0.5% quality bump there, we avoid vendor lock-in and isolate the face problem for a targeted fix later. The argument settles when we run controlled tests and publish the measured delta.
